did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens with Moses conveying to the Israelites the words as the Lord commanded, emphasizing his faithfulness in transmitting the command.
Did you know? Moses addresses the heads of the tribes in particular and presents the laws concerning vows and oaths.
Did you know? The Torah states that anyone who makes a vow or takes an oath must fulfill everything he has said and must not break his word.
Did you know? When a young woman is in her father’s house, her father’s silence on the day he hears her vow allows it to stand; if he objects that same day, the vow is annulled.
Did you know? Likewise, regarding the vows of a married woman, her husband’s silence on the day he hears them is considered consent, while annulling them that same day cancels the vow.
Did you know? The vow of a widow or divorcee remains in force, because in the situation described in the verse, there is no father or husband to annul it.
Did you know? The verse makes clear that a husband may uphold or annul certain vows and binding obligations of his wife, especially vows intended to afflict her.
Did you know? If the husband remains silent for a long time and then annuls the vow, the Torah holds him responsible for the guilt resulting from his delayed annulment.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the Torah summarizes that these laws concern two central family relationships: a man and his wife, and a father and his daughter in her youth while she is in her father’s house.
